blocks.prompt: The Scarecrow That Has to Keep Moving
blocks.text: A scarecrow is a person made of straw. Farmers put one in the field to keep birds away from the seeds. A scarecrow wears old clothes. The clothes flap in the wind. From far away, the flapping looks like a real person moving. Birds do not want to land near a person. But crows are clever. If the scarecrow stands still in the same spot for many days, the crows work it out. They land right on its hat. So farmers move the scarecrow. They give it a new coat. A scarecrow that changes keeps working.

blocks.prompt: The Oldest Trick on the Farm
blocks.text: Scarecrows are older than almost anything else on a farm. Three thousand years ago, farmers in Japan hung rags, old fish bones, and hair on sticks and set them smoking. The smell was terrible. Birds and deer stayed away. The Japanese word for scarecrow is kakashi, which comes from an older word meaning something that stinks. The straw figure with a hat came much later. In England, the scarecrow was once a job instead of an object. Farmers hired children called bird scarers. A bird scarer walked the fields from dawn until dark, banging two pieces of wood together and throwing stones at anything that landed. When farm workers became hard to find, farmers stuffed a sack with straw, gave it an old coat, and stood it up in the field instead. Here is the problem every farmer runs into. A scarecrow works because a bird thinks it might be a person. Crows are patient. They watch from the far end of the row. After a few days of nothing happening, they stop believing it, and then they perch on its shoulders. The best scarecrow is the one that gets moved.

blocks.prompt: Why the Scarecrow Stops Working
blocks.text: A scarecrow is a bluff. It has no muscles, no voice, and no way to chase anything. It works only if a bird looks at it and guesses wrong. For a day or two the bird plays it safe and feeds somewhere else, because being wrong about a predator is expensive and moving to the next field is not. Then the bird starts testing. It lands at the far end of the row. Nothing happens. The next morning it lands closer. Still nothing. Scientists call this habituation, which means learning to ignore a signal that never turns out to matter. Habituation is one of the simplest kinds of learning, and almost every animal with a nervous system can do it. Crows are especially quick. Crows are unusually intelligent birds. They bend sticks into hooks to fish grubs out of wood, they remember which people have treated them badly, and they pass that information along to other crows. A figure standing in the same posture, in the same corner, wearing the same coat every single morning is exactly the sort of thing a crow can file away as scenery. Farmers have always known this, even without a word for it. The old advice is to move the scarecrow every few days, change its clothes, and shift its arms into a new pose. Modern farms do the same thing with newer tools: reflective ribbon that spins in the wind, gas cannons that fire at random times, kites cut in the shape of a hawk, and lasers swept across the crop at dawn. Every one of them works better when it is unpredictable. The scarecrow's real job was never to look frightening. It was to look like something that might change its mind.

blocks.prompt: The Bluff in the Field
blocks.text: Nobody knows who built the first scarecrow, but the idea is at least three thousand years old and it appeared in several places independently. Egyptian farmers along the Nile stretched nets over wooden frames to protect wheat from flocks of quail. Greek growers carved rough wooden figures and set them among the vines, and Roman farmers carried the habit north into Europe. In Japan, the earliest versions were not figures at all. Farmers hung rags, hair, and old fish on poles and left them smoldering, trusting smell and smoke rather than shape. The Japanese word for a scarecrow is still kakashi, which comes from an older term for something that stinks. The straw man in a battered hat, the figure most people picture, came much later. In medieval England the scarecrow was a job rather than an object. Children were hired as bird scarers, walking the fields from first light, banging wooden clappers and slinging stones at anything that settled on the seed. After the plague of the fourteenth century emptied the countryside of workers, farmers replaced the children with sacks of straw dressed in cast off clothing, and the word scarecrow slid from a job title onto a thing. What makes the scarecrow genuinely interesting is that it fails, and that it fails for a reason worth understanding. A scarecrow contains no threat whatsoever. It is a bluff aimed at an animal's judgment. Birds treat an unfamiliar upright shape as a possible predator and keep their distance, which is sensible when the cost of guessing wrong is being eaten. But birds also gather evidence. A crow will land at the edge of the field, wait, watch, and creep nearer over several days. When nothing ever happens, the fear drains out of the shape. Biologists call this habituation, and it is the reason no single bird scaring device has ever kept working on its own. Crows sharpen the problem. Researchers at the University of Washington wore a distinctive mask while briefly trapping and banding wild crows, then walked the campus in that mask for years afterward. The crows scolded and mobbed that face on sight, and so did crows that had never been trapped, having learned the warning from the flock. A bird that can recognize one human face and broadcast it to its neighbors is not going to be fooled for long by a coat on a stick. So the trick was never the costume. It was the change. Farmers who move their scarecrows, redress them, and pair them with noise get months of use. Farmers who plant one and forget it get about a week, and then a crow sitting on the hat.

blocks.prompt: A Coat on a Stick: The Invention That Only Works While It Is Believed
blocks.text: Consider what a scarecrow actually is. It is a coat, a hat, and a bundle of straw arranged in roughly the shape of a human being and left standing in a field. It cannot move on its own, make a sound, or harm anything at all. Every scarecrow that has ever worked has worked entirely inside the mind of a bird, and the moment the bird changes its mind, the object becomes laundry on a pole. Few human inventions depend so completely on being misunderstood. The idea is ancient, and it was invented more than once. Egyptian farmers along the Nile rigged nets on wooden frames to keep flocks of quail off the wheat. Greek growers carved crude wooden figures and set them among the vines, and Roman farmers carried the practice north into Europe. In Japan the earliest versions were not figures at all. Farmers hung rags, hair, and old fish on poles and left them smoldering, trusting smell and smoke rather than shape, and the Japanese word for scarecrow, kakashi, still carries that origin in an older term for something that stinks. In medieval England, a scarecrow was a person. Children were employed as bird scarers, patrolling the fields from dawn with wooden clappers and pockets full of stones. Only after the labor shortages that followed the fourteenth century plague did English farmers begin dressing sacks of straw and standing them in the fields instead, and the word slid quietly from a job title onto an object. That object has one structural weakness, and it is not a flaw that better craftsmanship could repair. A scarecrow is a bluff, and bluffs expire. A bird approaching a field runs a fast calculation. An unfamiliar upright shape might be a predator, and the penalty for being wrong about a predator is death, so avoidance is cheap insurance. But birds also gather evidence. A crow lands at the far edge, waits, and watches. Nothing happens. The next day it lands nearer. Nothing happens again. Within a week the shape has been reclassified as scenery. Biologists call this habituation, the gradual fading of a response to a stimulus that never delivers consequences. It is among the simplest forms of learning, and virtually every animal with a nervous system does it. Crows do it faster and better than most, because crows are extraordinarily good at learning the specifics of their surroundings. In a long running study at the University of Washington, researchers wore a distinctive mask while capturing and banding wild crows, released the birds, and then continued walking the campus in that mask for years. The crows scolded and mobbed that face on sight. So did crows that had never been captured, and later, crows that had not been hatched at the time. The knowledge moved through the population socially, from bird to bird and from parent to offspring. An animal capable of that is not going to be permanently deceived by a stationary coat. The consequence is that every serious bird control method is really a method of managing habituation. Farmers today use reflective ribbon, propane cannons that fire at irregular intervals, kites cut in the silhouette of a hawk, drones, lasers swept across the crop at dawn, and recordings of distress calls. Each one works, and each one stops working, usually within weeks, unless it is moved, varied, randomized, or backed occasionally by something real. The old farming advice was identical long before anyone had the vocabulary for it: shift the scarecrow, change its clothes, give it a new pose. The scarecrow's job was never to be frightening. It was to stay uncertain.
